newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EU aspirants exempt from EMU strings - Van den Broek.
newsitem.headline: EU aspirants exempt from EMU strings - Van den Broek.

text.p: The European Union's (EU) commissioner for enlargement said on Friday countries from eastern Europe wishing to join the EU will not need to meet criteria on the single European currency in order to become full members but may have to wait until 2002 to join.

"The obligation that (applicant countries) accept by joining the union is that as soon as the EMU (European Monetary Union) criteria are fulfilled then they will join the single currency," Hans Van den Broek told Reuters in an interview.
"But that need not be the case at the moment of membership of the European Union."
Van den Broek was speaking during a two-day visit to Budapest to review Hungary's economic and political progress towards European integration.

An EU summit in Dublin last weekend paved the way for an intense round of negotiations over the next six months to draw up a new treaty aimed at helping the Union cope with an influx of new members, mainly from former communist eastern Europe.

The 11 applicants have been told that formal talks on their membership are due in one year's time, six months or so after the preparation of the new treaty needed to help the EU cope with the new members by simplifying decision-making and reducing the use of national vetoes.
However, Van den Broek echoed the warning made last month by the European Commission's representative in Hungary, Hans Beck, that no applicant should expect to join the Union before 2002
"I certainly believe that is a realistic statement," he said. "But what is of overriding importance is that the candidates determine the calendar themselves.

"As soon as they are ready with their economic preparations and with their fulfilling the political conditons for full membership there will be no reason for the European Union to delay the enlargement."

Van den Broek added that the final timetable for entry will also be determined by how quickly the parliaments of the 15 member states and of the candidate countries ratify the result of the accession negotiations.
He said that the EU may decide to open negotiations with some applicants ahead of others.

"That decision could be taken," he said. "That scenario will be decided as soon as the European Commission has reported to the European Council about the state of preparation about each candidate next year."
"What is certain is that they will not conclude negotiations all at the same time, in other words they will not join the European Union all at the same time," he said.
Hungary, Poland, the Czech republic and Slovenia are seen by diplomats and analysts as the favourites for early EU entry.

Van den Broek said Hungary had made "tremendous efforts" in reforming its political and economic instituions and mechanisms while Poland's recent decision to abolish import tariffs on oil imports by 2001 was also a step forward.
"I would not overdramatise this one point," he said. "That was one of the very important issues in the whole planning towards price liberalisation which has now found a solution."
Van den Broek said that while certain economic sectors may need time to adjust to European norms, all new members will have to abide by the rules of the internal market.
"Without any doubt it is not only in the interest of the European Union by keeping it strong, it is also in the interests of these (applicant) countries," he said.
"If you want to be competitive, to survive in an open market without borders you need to have a full fledged fuctioning market economy.
"One should not have the impression that the rules of the game themselves are negotiable," Van den Broek said.
